Presbyterianism
prez-bih-TEER-ee-an-iz-um
noun (a form of church government)
From the Greek presbyteros (elder); the system of church government by elders and graded assemblies (sessions, presbyteries, synods, general assemblies), held by the Presbyterian and Reformed churches.

📖 Biblical Definition

Presbyterianism is the system of church government in which the church is ruled by elders (Greek presbyteroi) gathered in graded assemblies—the local session, the regional presbytery, the broader synod, and the general assembly—held by the Presbyterian and many Reformed churches as the New Testament pattern. It rests on several biblical convictions: that the church is governed not by a single bishop nor by the congregation alone but by a plurality of elders; that elders were ordained in every church (Acts 14:23) and in every city (Titus 1:5); that the office is conferred with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery; and that disputed matters are settled by assemblies of apostles and elders gathered together, as at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15). The dictionary treats Presbyterianism with respect as a serious and biblically-argued polity within the Reformed family, the government of the Westminster churches and the Church of Scotland. Yet the dictionary, holding the 1689 Baptist Confession and the congregational polity of the Baptists, differs from Presbyterianism on the question of church government and on the related matter of the subjects of baptism. Where Presbyterianism gathers local churches under the binding authority of higher courts, the Baptist tradition holds to the independence of the local congregation under Christ, governed by its own elders and members, associating with other churches voluntarily rather than under a binding hierarchy of assemblies. The dictionary marks this as a difference among brethren who hold the same gospel of sovereign grace and the same Reformed doctrine: Presbyterians and Reformed Baptists are agreed on the great matters of salvation and divided on the polity and the subjects of baptism, contending as friends over the New Testament pattern of the church.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Church government by elders in graded assemblies (session, presbytery, synod, general assembly), held by Presbyterian and Reformed churches as the New Testament pattern (Acts 14:23; 15:6); respected by the dictionary, which holds the Baptist congregational polity.

expand to see more

PRESBYTERIANISM, noun. [Greek presbyteros, elder.] Church government by elders in graded assemblies.

Ruled by sessions, presbyteries, synods, and general assemblies.

Rests on rule by a plurality of elders ordained in every church (Acts 14:23).

The office conferred by the laying on of the hands of the presbytery (1 Timothy 4:14).

Disputed matters settled by assemblies of elders, as at Jerusalem (Acts 15:6).

📖 Key Scripture

Ac 14:23 — "And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed."

1 Ti 4:14 — "Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery."

Ac 15:6 — "And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter."

Tit 1:5 — "For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the dictionary, holding Baptist congregational polity, differs from Presbyterianism on church government and the subjects of baptism, as a difference among brethren in the same gospel.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter at issue is not a corruption to be rebutted but a difference among brethren who hold the same gospel. The dictionary respects Presbyterianism as a serious, biblically-argued polity within the Reformed family, the government of the Westminster churches and the Kirk of Scotland, resting on real New Testament evidence for rule by a plurality of elders, the laying on of hands by the presbytery, and the settling of disputes by assemblies of elders. It is no light or unscriptural scheme, and the dictionary contends with it as with friends, not foes.

Yet the dictionary, holding the 1689 Baptist Confession and the congregational polity of the Baptists, differs on the question of church government and the related question of baptism. Where Presbyterianism binds local churches under the authority of higher courts—presbyteries and assemblies—the Baptist tradition holds to the independence of the local congregation under Christ its only Head, governed by its own elders and members, and associating with sister churches voluntarily rather than under a binding hierarchy. And where Presbyterianism baptizes the infant children of believers, the Baptist baptizes believers only. The dictionary marks these as differences among those agreed on the great gospel of sovereign grace and the doctrines of the Reformed faith—Presbyterians and Reformed Baptists contending as brethren over the New Testament pattern of the church, not over the way of salvation.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Greek presbyteros (elder, older man); the polity of rule by elders (presbyteroi) gathered in a “presbytery” and graded assemblies.

expand to see more

Presbyteros, Greek, an elder, the officer who rules in this polity.

Presbyterion, Greek, “presbytery,” the body of elders (1 Timothy 4:14).

The graded courts: session, presbytery, synod, general assembly.

Rests on the New Testament pattern of rule by a plurality of elders.

Distinguished from episcopal (bishop-ruled) and congregational (independent) polities.

Usage

"The teacher described Presbyterianism as rule by elders in graded assemblies, the polity of the Westminster churches."

"He respected the Presbyterian polity while holding the Baptist independence of the local congregation."

"She saw Presbyterians and Reformed Baptists as brethren agreed on the gospel, divided on church government and baptism."
